title: How to Meet a Credit Card Minimum Spend Without Overspending
summary: Ways to meet a credit card minimum spend, what each method costs per $1,000 charged, which purchases count toward your bonus, and how to avoid losing it.
body_markdown:
New rewards cards make you earn the sign-up bonus by charging a set amount in the first few months, with three months being the usual window. Chase's Sapphire Preferred, for one, was asking for[$5,000 in purchases in the first 3 months](https://creditcards.chase.com/rewards-credit-cards/sapphire/preferred) when we checked in October 2026. Moving spending you already had planned onto the new card gets most people there for nothing. Paying a fee to close the last stretch can be fine. It just has to be small next to the bonus, and on something you were buying anyway.


## What Counts Toward a Minimum Spend (and What Doesn't)


Purchases count. Most other things you can do with a card don't.


The fine print lists what's out. Chase's list, from the Sapphire Preferred page: no balance transfers, no cash advances, no person-to-person transfers, and nothing it treats as a "cash-like transaction," which takes in money orders, wire transfers, travelers checks and crypto. Amex comes at it from the other side. The Gold Card terms count[eligible purchases](https://www.americanexpress.com/en-us/credit-cards/apply/terms/personal/gold-card/25330-10-0) as goods and services, minus anything returned or credited back, and then list what's excluded: fees, interest, cash advances, person to person payments, travelers checks, "other cash equivalents" and a few more.


Annual fees don't count either. Neither does interest.


Yours will read a little differently, so give your own terms ten minutes. Also check when the clock started. That's the day the account opened, which can be well before the card is in your hands.


## Start With Spending You Already Have Planned


Start with what's already on the calendar. Say the car needs new tires next month, or there's a flight home for the holidays. Open the card a few weeks before that money goes out and a good chunk of the requirement takes care of itself, with money you'd have spent anyway.


After that, the boring stuff. Phone, internet, streaming and insurance take cards with most providers and don't charge extra for it. Point autopay at the new card for three months and it adds up faster than it looks.


## Ways to Meet the Minimum Spend, With What Each Costs


Some of these are free. Others charge a fee, and that fee is what the bonus really costs you if you go that route.


### Recurring Bills You Can Switch to the Card


Utilities, your phone plan, the gym, every subscription you forgot you had. Most take cards without a surcharge. A few utilities tack on a convenience fee for paying by card, which is worth a look on the payment page first.


### Prepaying Bills


Lots of insurers let you pay car or renters insurance six or twelve months at a time. Annual software and membership plans are the same idea. Same money, paid earlier.


### Rent and Mortgage


Few landlords take cards directly. Bill-pay services get around that by charging your card and paying the bill by check or bank transfer, and whether one will pay your landlord depends on the service. Plastiq charges[2.99%](https://www.plastiq.com/pricing) on card payments plus a small delivery fee each time, so call it $30 per $1,000. Mortgages are mostly a dead end. Servicers rarely take cards at all.


### Paying Taxes by Card


You can pay the IRS by card through one of its approved processors. The processor keeps the fee, not the IRS. On the IRS page (last updated September 2026),[Pay1040 is listed at 1.75% and ACI Payments at 1.85%](https://www.irs.gov/payments/pay-your-taxes-by-debit-or-credit-card) , $2.50 minimum on either, so roughly $18 per $1,000. It's a timing play, though. It only helps when a tax payment happens to fall inside your bonus window.


### Large Planned Purchases


Furniture, a new laptop, the trip you were booking regardless. For anyone who was already going to buy gold or silver, Pure takes major credit cards (American Express included) on[Pure Priority](https://help.collectpure.com/en/articles/15675316-what-is-pure-priority) orders. Those are items already verified and in storage, and they ship in 2 to 3 days after payment is confirmed. Card payments there carry a 2.9% surcharge, or $29 per $1,000. Pay by bank transfer and there's no surcharge at all. Whether the purchase counts toward a bonus, and which category it lands in, is up to your card's terms, so look before you count on it.


### Picking Up a Group Bill


Paying for a group dinner or a shared rental and letting friends pay you back costs nothing extra, as long as they repay you from a bank balance. One caution: Chase excludes person-to-person money transfers from bonus spend, so the purchase itself has to go on your card.

## Do the Math Before You Charge a Fee


Value the bonus at its plain cash-back or statement-credit amount, and hold the fee up against that. Don't use a best-case travel value.


Made-up numbers: the bonus is worth $750 in statement credit and you're $2,000 short with a month left. Run that $2,000 through something with a 2% fee and you've paid $40. If you were buying it anyway, $40 is what finishing the bonus cost you.


For something you hadn't planned, the cost is the whole purchase.


That's the test for every row in the table. A fee-bearing method only makes sense for spending that was already going to happen. Among those, pick the smaller fee. And pay the statement off in full. A month of interest on a few thousand dollars can cost more than any fee on this list.


## What Can Get a Bonus Taken Back


A bonus isn't locked in just because you crossed the number. On the Sapphire Preferred, Chase's terms want the account open and not in default at the moment the bonus posts. Returns can bite too. Amex subtracts returns and other credits from what counts, so if you return the thing you bought to clear the bar, you may find yourself back under it.


Issuers also keep broad discretion. Amex, for instance, reserves the right in its benefit terms to reverse statement credits whenever it decides, in its sole discretion, there's been["abuse, misuse, or gaming"](https://www.americanexpress.com/en-us/credit-cards/apply/terms/personal/gold-card/25330-10-0) . That's written about statement credits, not sign-up bonuses. You still get a sense of how much room issuers keep for themselves.


In practice, the purchases issuers flag look like cash. Steer clear of anything in the excluded list above, and of routing money back to yourself through the card.


## Track Your Progress


Most issuer apps show progress toward the bonus on the account page. Where the app is silent, tally posted purchases yourself and go a bit past the number. Anything still pending on deadline day might post late, and a purchase on the final day can fall outside the window. Put the date in your calendar when you open the account.
